This site holds the AWS-focused sessions being developed for GSB 5544. It exists so collaborators can see, in one place, **what has been built so far** and **what students will actually do** in each session. Every document is rendered here as a web page and is also available as a downloadable notebook or as a one-click Google Colab link.

::: {.callout-note title="No AWS account is needed"}
Every session uses public datasets from the [Registry of Open Data on AWS](https://registry.opendata.aws/). Students read from S3 anonymously with `boto3`, so there is nothing to sign up for and nothing that can generate a bill.
:::

## Status at a glance

| Session | Topic | Status | Student-facing documents |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Data Bigger Than Your Laptop: measuring capacity, S3 vocabulary, and extracting only what you need from NOAA weather data | **Complete draft**, ready for review | Pre-class reading, topics-of-practice notebook, practice activity, solutions for both |
| 2+ | To be determined | Not started | |

## How a session is structured

Each session follows the same three-part pattern, so students always know what to expect.

1. **Pre-class reading** (`01_*.md`). A self-contained explainer with runnable code snippets. Students read it and run the code before class. It ends with a short reading check.
2. **Topics of practice** (`02_*.ipynb`). An in-class, fill-in-the-blank walkthrough of every function introduced in the reading. Blanks are marked `____`. The instructor version has the blanks filled in.
3. **Practice activity** (`03_*.ipynb`). A business scenario with numbered questions and empty code cells. Students work through it in class or as homework. The solutions version has every cell completed.

The two notebooks are generated from a single source file, `build_notebooks.py`, so the student and solutions versions never drift apart. Editing the source and re-running the script regenerates all four notebooks.

## Session 1 · Data Bigger Than Your Laptop

### What students will learn

By the end of Session 1, students can:

- Measure how much RAM their own machine actually has available, and explain why "total" is not "available" and why disk is not memory.
- Read and reason in the units of data (KB through PB) and estimate whether a file will fit in pandas before trying to load it.
- Use the core AWS vocabulary: region, S3, bucket, object, key, prefix, and anonymous (unsigned) access.
- Connect to a public S3 bucket without an account, list objects, read an object's size from metadata alone, and peek at a file with a byte-range request.
- Extract a single station's full history rather than a whole year of global data, filter it at the source, transform it, and plot it.

### Dataset

All exercises use the **NOAA GHCN-Daily** dataset in the public `noaa-ghcn-pds` bucket. The by-year files are multi-gigabyte and will not fit on a laptop, which is the point. The by-station files are small enough to pull and analyze.

### What students will do, in order

**Before class: the pre-class reading.** Students work through six sections and answer a five-question reading check:

1. What your machine actually has
2. The units of data
3. The vocabulary of AWS
4. Reading from S3 without an account
5. Extraction strategy: filter at the source
6. Where this goes next

**In class: the topics-of-practice notebook.** A guided, fill-in-the-blank tour of the same material, one function at a time:

- A. What your machine actually has
- B. The units of data
- C. The vocabulary of AWS
- D. Connect without an account
- E. Read a size without reading the file
- F. Peek at a file with a range request
- G. Extract one station, not one year
- H. Transform
- I. Bring the visual

**In class or as homework: the practice activity.** Students play an inventory planner for a beverage distributor with two markets, San Luis Obispo and Phoenix, and need each market's weather history before anyone builds a demand model. Eleven questions across four sets:

- **Set 1 · Capacity.** Measure the machine, estimate how many rows fit, and total a decade of by-year files against available RAM.
- **Set 2 · Vocabulary in action.** List prefixes, explain why a "folder" is not a folder, and read file metadata without downloading.
- **Set 3 · Extraction.** Write a reusable `load_station()` function, pull both markets, count hot days per year, and compute monthly rainfall.
- **Set 4 · Visualize and interpret.** Chart both markets, write the business read, and (stretch) do it the wrong way on purpose to see why extraction strategy matters.

### What students need installed

```bash
pip install psutil boto3 pandas matplotlib
```

Colab already has all four. Locally, any Python 3.9+ with Jupyter works.
